title: Bulk structural solids that are both near their ideal strength and damage-tolerant

concept.text: The innovation would be a bulk structural material that withstands stresses approaching the intrinsic strength of its crystal lattice while remaining resistant to the growth of cracks. It would also need to be reproducibly manufacturable, practically joinable and affordable for a defined structural application. The aim is to combine exceptional strength with the ability to carry loads safely despite realistic damage.

Ideal strength is the stress at which an initially perfect crystal lattice becomes unstable under a specified loading condition. Real materials can yield or fracture earlier because of dislocations, surfaces and flaws. Strength measures the stress a material withstands; fracture toughness describes its resistance to crack propagation. A very strong whisker, monolayer, ribbon or fiber therefore establishes only part of the desired capability. The target requires the combination in substantial load-bearing sections, including the effects of processing and joining.

significance.text: The revolutionary potential lies in changing the compromise that governs many safety-critical structures. High strength helps resist permanent deformation, but a component also needs sufficient fracture resistance to prevent a small crack from causing catastrophic failure. Combining near-ideal usable strength with damage tolerance could allow engineers to exploit much more of a material's intrinsic load-bearing capability without sacrificing resistance to crack growth.

Conditional engineering synthesis: in structures governed mainly by strength, the combination could reduce the amount of material required, lower structural mass or increase allowable loads. Pressure vessels and other highly stressed components are plausible beneficiaries. Those gains would depend on density, stiffness, buckling, fatigue, service environment and joint performance. Higher strength would not necessarily improve mass, span and failure load together, especially where stiffness or stability already controls the design.

Conditional downstream possibility: extreme systems such as a space tether could benefit from exceptional structural material, but this breakthrough alone would not establish their feasibility. Such systems would still require separate analysis of specific strength, length-dependent reliability, environmental exposure, manufacturing, connections and deployment.

Carbon-nanotube or graphene structures could fall within this innovation if they met its bulk mechanical and practical requirements. Retaining the electrical conductivity of individual tubes or sheets would be an additional achievement. The supplied CNT study describes electrical transport as depending on inter-tube resistance and the continuity of the conducting network, so solving strength and fracture resistance does not automatically solve conductivity transfer from the constituent to the assembled material.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this record is reproducibly combining near-ideal usable strength with structural crack tolerance in bulk sections. Suppressing the defects that permit early yielding is only part of the problem: deformation mechanisms can also help a material accommodate stress around a crack. The challenge is to prevent premature failure while retaining mechanisms that resist crack growth. The strength–toughness conflict is a general materials-design difficulty, rather than an absolute prohibition; the supplied Ritchie abstract also describes strategies for overcoming it within particular material classes.

Scaling introduces a separate barrier. Small specimens can avoid some defects yet still fail through surface-mediated processes before reaching lattice instability. The iron paper discusses whisker strength limited by dislocation nucleation at free surfaces. Assembling nanoscale constituents into larger structures also requires effective load transfer across their interfaces. Strong CNT films and fibers demonstrate progress in that direction, but their strength measurements do not establish bulk fracture toughness.

Engineering synthesis: a complete solution must preserve the mechanical combination through substantial section thickness, manufacturing variability and practical joints. It must also meet a defined production-cost target. Exceptional performance in a selected thin specimen would not resolve those requirements. The supplied literature establishes the research goal and important barriers, but does not establish that the full capability was absent across the entire field as of 1 November 2026.

current_state.text: Morris, Guo, Krenn and Kim, ISIJ International 41, 599–611 (2001), provide historical estimates for iron of approximately 10.5 GPa ideal cleavage stress and 6.5 GPa ideal shear strength. The shear value was inferred using a modulus-based relation rather than directly computed in that work. These are material- and loading-dependent ideal-strength comparisons, not measured strengths of a finished structural product or universal targets for other materials.

Ritchie, Nature Materials 10, 817–822, published on 24 October 2011, explains why both strength and toughness matter for structural applications and why achieving them together is generally difficult. It also discusses approaches that overcome the conflict within particular material classes. The supplied review had access to a subscription preview and abstract rather than the full article, so this source supports the broad design motivation without establishing the detailed limits of every approach or the state of the field in 2026.

Wang and colleagues, Nature Communications 17, 8231, published on 2 July 2026, report CNT fibers and thin films reaching 12.5 GPa absolute strength and 7.5 N·tex−1 specific strength. The 12.5 GPa result concerns a ribbon approximately 0.15 μm thick; the supplied review distinguishes it from a rolled sample reported at 11.7 GPa. The article reports axial electrical conductivity of 2.4–2.8×10^6 S·m−1, summarized approximately as 3×10^6 S·m−1. It places the strength near the lower end of a cited 13–80 GPa range for individual CNTs. That constituent range is background reported by the article; its underlying references were not independently assessed in the supplied review.

The CNT work extends beyond a short-gauge fiber record. It describes long films, overlapping-strip tests and similar strengths at gauge lengths of 2, 10, 20 and 30 mm, with slightly lower strengths at 40 and 50 mm. It also reports a load demonstration using a 75 cm rope. These results show meaningful progress in length and assembly, while the reported dimensions and tests do not establish standard bulk fracture toughness, tough bulk plate, structural-metal-scale production or affordability.

The supplied review assessed the CNT headline results from the article prose; figures, videos and raw source data were not visually or independently inspected. The retained HTML records an October 2026 correction to source-data labeling, without reporting a revision to the headline strengths. These limits constrain independent verification but do not show that the reported results are false.

The U.S. Department of Energy Basic Energy Sciences historical EFRC grand-challenge page identifies materials operating at theoretical limits of strength and fracture resistance as a research goal. Its framing includes past EFRC activity from 2009–2024, so it cannot establish that the complete goal remained open in 2026. No bounded contemporary search record was supplied. The dated achievements above can therefore be retained, while field-wide availability of the full bulk, damage-tolerant, joinable and affordable capability as of 1 November 2026 remains unverified.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: specimens should have centimeter-scale load-bearing dimensions together with explicitly specified bulk section thickness, and results should be reproduced across more than one processing batch. Before testing, investigators should declare the required fraction of ideal strength, the relevant material and crystal orientation, tensile or shear loading mode, specimen geometry, service conditions and statistical acceptance rules. A numerical strength-to-ideal ratio would make the target more discriminating than merely requiring values of the same order. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Centimeter-scale bulk specimens reproduced across multiple processing batches

completion_criteria.text: Proposed combined mechanical test: representative material from the same reproducible process should meet both the declared near-ideal strength target and valid standard fracture-toughness measurements against a predeclared structural damage-tolerance criterion. Specimen dimensions and the selected toughness metric must support a valid interpretation for that material and geometry. The strength result should not come solely from a thin ribbon while the toughness result comes from a materially different, lower-strength product.
completion_criteria.label: Same-process material meets declared strength and damage-tolerance criteria

completion_criteria.text: The strength comparison must match the tested material and loading mode. The 2001 iron estimates of approximately 10.5 GPa in cleavage and 6.5 GPa in shear are useful historical reference points, with the latter inferred rather than directly calculated in that paper. They do not define a universal completion threshold, and cleavage stress should not be treated as interchangeable with every tensile or shear strength measurement.
completion_criteria.label: Ideal-strength comparisons match tested material and loading mode

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical validation: demonstrate representative joints, including their effects on strength and crack resistance, and assess production against a stated cost target and output scale. Independent replication should reproduce the combined properties with reported specimen selection, batch variation and measurement uncertainty. Application-specific qualification should define the demonstrated bounds for fatigue, temperature, environment, loading rate and allowable damage. Finite testing would establish performance within those bounds rather than universal reliability under every service condition.
completion_criteria.label: Joint performance, production viability and application bounds independently validated

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis — MAS-03, General atomically precise covalent construction: precise control of atomic structure could help manage defects or interfaces relevant to strength, but it is a manufacturing capability with a different endpoint. Atomic precision alone would not demonstrate bulk crack tolerance, practical joints or acceptable structural cost. Conversely, MAS-02 could potentially be achieved through processing that is not generally atomically precise.

Roster synthesis — MAS-04, A reliable map from a property specification to a makeable material: such a design capability could help discover compositions and processing routes that balance strength and toughness. MAS-04 concerns the general ability to move from a specification to a manufacturable material; MAS-02 concerns experimentally achieving one particular demanding combination of properties.

Roster synthesis — MAS-05, Structural solids that remain engineering materials after fusion-level atomic displacement: both require usable structural performance despite defects. MAS-05 specifically concerns retention of engineering properties after severe irradiation damage. Near-ideal strength and crack tolerance before irradiation would not establish radiation durability, and radiation durability would not establish near-ideal strength.

Roster synthesis — MAS-07, Programmable growth of load-bearing solids: controlled growth could provide a route to large shapes or useful internal architectures. MAS-07 concerns how load-bearing matter is formed, while MAS-02 requires a particular combination of intrinsic strength, fracture resistance and practical structural performance. Either could be demonstrated without completing the other.

Roster synthesis — MAS-09, Structural metals that fully recover from macroscopic fracture in service: damage tolerance resists crack growth and maintains useful load capacity in the presence of damage; recovery from fracture restores a component after macroscopic separation or cracking. These are distinct capabilities. A near-ideal, crack-resistant solid need not heal, and a self-repairing metal need not approach its ideal lattice strength.

Roster synthesis — MAS-01, Ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductivity in a manufacturable solid: retaining high ordinary electrical conductivity in a CNT or graphene structure is distinct from achieving superconductivity. Electrical performance may be an optional additional objective for MAS-02, but neither high mechanical strength nor high conventional conductivity establishes the superconducting capability in MAS-01.

unresolved_issues: Whether any material met the complete bulk, near-ideal-strength, damage-tolerant, joinable and economically practical combination as of 1 November 2026 remains unverified because no bounded contemporary search record was supplied.
A quantitative definition of near-ideal strength remains to be selected for a specific material, orientation and loading mode; no universal fraction is established by these inputs.
Bulk section dimensions, a structural damage-tolerance acceptance criterion, production scale and an affordability target remain unspecified.
The supplied CNT evidence does not establish standard bulk fracture toughness, representative structural-joint performance or structural-scale production economics.
The CNT article's cited 13–80 GPa individual-tube range and raw experimental evidence were not independently verified in the supplied review.
Ritchie's full article was not available in the supplied review; interpretation here is limited to the accessible preview and abstract.

brief.title: Materials that carry extreme loads despite cracks
possible: Engineers could build load-bearing parts that use nearly all the strength their atoms can provide while resisting the growth of cracks. The goal is thick, practical components that can be made reliably, joined together and afforded.
why: Pressure vessels and other heavily loaded components could carry more weight or use less material. Strength prevents permanent bending or stretching; resistance to crack growth helps keep a small flaw from causing sudden failure.

sources.who: J. W. Morris Jr., Z. Guo, C. R. Krenn and Y.-H. Kim
sources.showed: They estimated the strength limits of perfect iron crystals and examined ways to improve steel’s resistance to cracking.
sources.quote:
The elastic instability of the crystal lattice sets
an absolute upper bound on the strength a material can
have, the ideal strength.
sources.cited_for: It explains ideal strength: the limit at which a perfect arrangement of atoms becomes unstable.
sources.not_established: Calculations for perfect crystals do not demonstrate a practical bulk material that also resists crack growth.

sources.showed: His review explains the conflict between strength and toughness, meaning resistance to crack growth, and describes materials that overcome it within their classes.
sources.quote: We show how these new and natural materials can defeat the conflict of strength versus toughness and achieve unprecedented levels of damage tolerance within their respective material classes.
sources.cited_for: Strength and crack resistance can coexist, but combining them requires deliberate material design.
sources.not_established: Overcoming the trade-off within a material class does not establish near-ideal strength in practical bulk components.

sources.showed: They aligned and tightly packed carbon nanotubes, tiny hollow carbon structures, to make thin ribbons with a reported pulling strength of 12.5 gigapascals.
sources.quote: In the case of scouring, CNTs became straight, aligned, and densely packed.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates progress in transferring the strength of tiny tubes into larger assemblies.
sources.not_established: Thin ribbons and rope demonstrations do not establish crack resistance in thick components, practical joints or affordable production.

sources.who: U.S. Department of Energy, Basic Energy Sciences
sources.showed: The programme identified materials reaching theoretical limits of strength and crack resistance as a research goal.
sources.cited_for: It establishes the combined properties as an explicit research goal.
sources.not_established: A research goal does not demonstrate a material that achieves it.

shown: Wang and colleagues reported unusually strong carbon nanotube ribbons made by spraying ethanol while stretching them. They also tested longer assemblies and demonstrated a rope carrying a load.
missing: Thick load-bearing pieces still need to combine near-ideal strength with measured resistance to crack growth.
The combined properties need to survive repeated manufacturing batches and practical joints.
Production needs to meet a defined cost and output target for a particular structural use.

milestones.label: Centimeter-scale bulk pieces with repeatable properties
milestones.explanation: Centimeter-scale pieces with specified thickness would have to meet a declared strength target across manufacturing batches. This would establish repeatability beyond selected thin specimens.

milestones.label: Strength and crack resistance in the same material
milestones.explanation: Material from the same process would have to pass both the strength target and valid standard crack-resistance tests. This would establish that the desired properties coexist.

milestones.label: Strength measured against the right theoretical limit
milestones.explanation: The ideal-strength comparison would have to match the tested material, atomic orientation and type of loading. This would make the claim of approaching the material’s limit meaningful.

milestones.label: Joints, production and service limits independently validated
milestones.explanation: Independent tests would have to confirm the combined properties, joint performance, production cost and scale, and application-specific service limits. This would establish where engineers could safely use the material.

uncertain: How close to ideal strength is close enough remains to be defined for each material and loading condition.
Required thickness, acceptable damage, production scale and affordability still need specific targets.
Removing defects can raise strength while also removing ways for a material to relieve stress around a crack.

page.title: Bulk solids at ideal strength with crack-growth resistance
page.definition: A manufactured bulk solid combines strength at the instability limit of its corresponding perfect crystal lattice with resistance to crack growth. The combination persists in a load-bearing component under a published damage-tolerance qualification, which establishes whether damaged structure can carry its required loads.

goal.need: The Austrian Academy of Sciences’ USMS project reported pearlitic steel wire strength of 6.3 GPa and identified fracture toughness as necessary for retaining strength despite flaws or cracks. Its comparison below illustrates the remaining strength gap. The project ran from 1 March 2014 to 28 February 2019; these are historical project estimates, not a survey of current materials.

figures.caption: Strength relative to theoretical strength in the USMS project summary
figures.note: The project summary does not supply specimen counts for this comparison.

completion.title: A bulk solid reaches lattice-limited strength in a component that passes damage-tolerance qualification.
completion.criterion: A manufactured load-bearing component has sections thicker than 1 mm whose unnotched strength agrees, within experimental and calculation uncertainties, with the corresponding lattice-instability strength. The component, including joints where present, passes its applicable published damage-tolerance qualification for service loads, crack sizes, fatigue spectrum and environment. Strength and valid fracture-mechanics specimens represent the component’s production process and load-bearing section. For transport aircraft, the damage-tolerance evaluation is specified in 14 CFR 25.571(b).
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional combined test; the numerical section threshold is adapted from DARPA INTACT’s ceramic-coupon milestone.
completion.basis: DOE/BESAC grand challenges, DARPA INTACT targets, ASTM fracture standards and FAA damage-tolerance rules were searched. No material-general combined test or fraction defining near-ideal strength was found. This conservative test pairs the material-specific lattice-instability limit with an existing application qualification. INTACT’s greater-than-1-mm coupon threshold supplies an explicit section benchmark; its use beyond ceramics is an Atlas choice.

milestones.title: A small crystal reaches its lattice-instability strength under a specified loading path.
milestones.criterion: Failure occurs at the calculated lattice-instability stress for the same composition, crystal orientation and loading path. On 4 December 2019, Nie et al. reported one ⟨100⟩ diamond nanoneedle tested through four successive fractures: at 60 nm diameter, its inferred local tensile strength was 125 GPa. This matched a 122 GPa Griffith estimate but remained below its calculated ideal strength of 225 GPa. That result does not satisfy the lattice-instability test.
milestones.set_by: The ideal-strength convention described by Morris et al., section 2, and applied in atomistic strength calculations; this is a physical limit, not a standardised experimental acceptance protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: The elastic instability of the crystal lattice sets an absolute upper bound on the strength a material can have, the ideal strength.

milestones.title: A manufactured section thicker than 1 mm retains its matched ideal strength.
milestones.criterion: Unnotched specimens representing a manufactured section thicker than 1 mm reach the material- and loading-specific ideal-strength reference. INTACT publishes the dimensional benchmark for ceramic coupons, but does not combine it with ideal strength. Wang et al., published on 2 July 2026, reported 12.5 GPa in carbon-nanotube ribbons about 0.15 μm thick. Their protocol tested 3–5 specimens per material and condition, usually at 10 mm gauge length. Those ribbons do not establish this bulk-strength milestone.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional bulk-strength test; searches found DARPA INTACT’s greater-than-1-mm ceramic-coupon milestone, but no material-general bulk ideal-strength acceptance test.

milestones.title: A bulk solid reaches lattice-limited strength and resists its application’s crack-driving force.
milestones.criterion: Unnotched specimens representing a bulk load-bearing section reach the matched ideal-strength reference. Sharp-cracked specimens from the same production process resist unstable extension at the crack-driving force required by the intended application’s published residual-strength load case. Fracture tests satisfy the applicable method’s validity conditions, such as ASTM E1820 for metallic materials or C1421 for advanced ceramics. Component qualification remains outstanding at this stage.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional combined coupon test; searches found ASTM fracture methods and application-specific residual-strength rules, but no material-general criterion combining them with ideal strength.

not_found: No material-general numerical definition of near-ideal strength or combined strength–toughness acceptance threshold was found.
No material-general qualification thresholds for joining, production volume or affordability were found.
The searched sources did not establish a result combining matched bulk ideal strength, valid fracture-resistance measurements and component damage-tolerance qualification.
The full 2007 BESAC report exceeded the browser’s size limit; DOE’s EFRC summary was accessible.
The 2026 Nature paper Ceramic-like strength and metallic toughness in a bulk metallic glass could not be opened.
Only the publisher summaries of ASTM E1820 and C1421 were accessible; their complete specimen-validity clauses were not.
